newsitem.title: USA: US scrap metal courts "isolation" over convention.
newsitem.headline: US scrap metal courts "isolation" over convention.

text.p: The huge scrap metal industry in the United States may get left out in the cold if it does not play an active role in shaping the Basle Convention on movement of hazardous waste, an industry gathering was told.

"The danger of not ratifying is to get isolated, but the danger of ratifying is to lose a certain freedom domestically," Jacques Moulins, corporate manager, environment, of Canada's Noranda Metallurgy Inc, said.

Moulins told delegates at the U.S. Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries Round Table here that 100 countries, including the influential European Union trading bloc, had signed the convention since it was drawn up in 1992 despite its bureaucratic nature, Moulins said. "Basle is here to stay," he said.
But four years on there was still "no clear definition of hazardous waste," Moulins said, adding that many types of scrap metal were still classified as hazardous waste.
"I do believe that the business activity we are in makes sense economically and environmentally. At the end of the day this will prevail," Moulins said.

A working group was reviewing which types of scrap should be included on the A list which banned exportation from developed to developing countries, and which should be included in the less stringently regulated B list.

Robert Stein of Louis Padnos Iron and Metal Co, Michigan, said the United States was often criticised for not taking an active role in shaping the Basle debate. "It's been brought up often that we should participate more than we have done," Stein said.

The United States is a huge recycler of copper and aluminum scrap in particular, and is a significant exporter of non-ferrous scrap, particularly to East Asian countries such as China which has signed the convention.
Scrap trade between the United States and Canada is currently governed by bilateral agreements.
